subject: NSP
excerpt: I don't understand why Intel funds a group that is against Windows95.
context: Gates writes to Intel's Andy Grove about Intel's Native Signal Processing software.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 277, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: Netscape discussions
excerpt: This kind of deal could be a big win win. Of course over time we will compete on servers but we can help them a lot in the meantime. We could even pay them money as part of the deal buying some piece of them or something.
context: Gates floats a cooperation deal with Netscape; the DOJ later used the Microsoft-Netscape talks of 1995 as evidence.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 22, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: RE: Netscape discussions
excerpt: This is very much along the lines of the discussions I've already initiated with Jim Barksdale. He seems to be favorably disposed to the discussions. Bottom line: if we go to war with each other, then other industry players will set the terms of engagement (e.g. Visa and MasterCard on processing fees; AT&T and MCI on network issues) and we both loose more than we gain.
context: A Microsoft business development executive reports on early talks with Netscape's CEO.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 22, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: Netscape meeting
excerpt: Our goals going into the meeting were (in priority order): 1. Establish Microsoft ownership of the Internet client platform for Win95.
context: Summary of a four-hour meeting between seven Microsoft people and Netscape's leadership.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 35, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: Steve Case - AOL
excerpt: I talked to him this afternoon. He said they are on a path to close with Netscape before the end of the month. I told him I wanted to convince him to pay a visit and really talk about our goals. I said I wasn't going to be able to put AOL in the Windows box except in the sense that with a few strings typed in the user would be able to connect to AOL.
context: Gates reports a call with AOL's Steve Case as AOL weighed Netscape's browser against Microsoft's.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 335, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: Some Thoughts on Netscape
excerpt: During this Thinkweek I had a chance to play with a number of Netscape products. This reinforced the impression that I think all of us share that Netscape is quite an impressive competitor. They are moving at full speed.
context: Gates circulates a memo after his Thinkweek assessing Netscape's product line.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 41, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: RE: Downloads of IE
excerpt: I think on the UI front and the technology front Netscape has taken the basic IE 4 idea and is executing on it far better than we are.
context: Gates, in a thread about AOL and Internet Explorer downloads, says Netscape is ahead on IE 4's own ideas.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 346, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: HTML "Openness"
excerpt: I think we want to make Trident extremely hard to clone. I think we want to patent elements of Trident. I think we want to make extensions to Trident on an ongoing basis. I reconcile this with our statements about HTML by saying that we need to have "tags" that we view as Office/Windows/Microsoft specific.
context: Gates on Trident, the browser engine behind Internet Explorer, and how far Microsoft should extend HTML.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 351, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: RE: AMD 3DX thoughts
excerpt: If Intel has a real problem with us supporting this then they will have to stop supporting Java Multimedia the way they are. I would gladly give up supporting this if they would back off from their work on JAVA which is terrible for Intel.
context: Gates links Microsoft's support for AMD's 3DX instructions to Intel's Java work.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 290, DOJ Antitrust Division

excerpt: 2. How do we wrest control of Java away from Sun? 3. How do we turn Java into just the latest, best way to write Windows applications?

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 58, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: Java schism
excerpt: Since we do want to run JAVA applets in the browser we have to provide some JAVA support there. It may be that some of the JAVA runtime should ONLY be available through the browser - like AWT versus our equivalent. I think restricting some things to the browser is an important idea that should be explored.
context: Gates on how to limit pure Java applications while still running applets in Internet Explorer.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 254, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: RE: IBM
excerpt: Overall we will never have the same relationship with IBM that we have with Compaq, Dell and even HP because of their software ambitions. I could deal with this just fine if they weren't such rabid JAVA backers.
context: Gates replies to Microsoft's head of OEM sales on how to approach IBM's PC business.

source.title: US v. Microsoft (1998), government trial exhibit 257, DOJ Antitrust Division

subject: [Googlers] Business communications in a complicated world

source.title: United States v. Google (search), trial exhibit UPX1101, published by the Department of Justice

subject: [Googlers] Business communications in a complicated world
excerpt: First, please write carefully and thoughtfully. We're an email and instant-messaging culture. We conduct much of our work online. We believe that information is good. But anything you write can become subject to review in legal discovery, misconstrued, or taken out of context, and may be used against you or us in ways you wouldn't expect.
context: A company-wide note from two senior Google leaders on how to write in email and chat while legal matters were pending.

source.title: United States v. Google (search), trial exhibit UPX1101, published by the Department of Justice

subject: Re: sale reductions
excerpt: Fundamentally the glue that seals DFP to GCN is AdX (that is why it is the second pillar of our three-pillared strategy). It is essentially teh DFP - AdSense backfill we bought DCLK for but with the features that will actually get pubs to put their inventory into our ecosystem (dynamic allocation, competitive bidding from other networks, etc.).
context: Mohan explains why the AdX exchange ties Google's publisher ad server to its ad network.

source.title: United States v. Google (ad tech), trial exhibit PTX0041, published by the Department of Justice

subject: Re: sale reductions
excerpt: I was the hatchet man at DCLK back in 2000-2001 during the dotcom bust so have lived through this painful period before on display before. The biggest mistake made back then was the "death by a thousand cuts" scenario. That is, every quarter layoffs were made and the next quarter revenue shrank a bit more (because we didnt have the resources to keep the footprint in tact) and then more cuts were made until the business needed to be resurrected by a private equity firm.
context: Neal Mohan, then at DoubleClick inside Google, argues against deep cuts to the display ads business.

source.title: United States v. Google (ad tech), trial exhibit PTX0041, published by the Department of Justice

subject: Re: OpenX Market Launches!
excerpt: OpenX is the only relatively smaller player to offer the same three-pillared approach to the display market as us, Yahoo, MSFT and AOL - platform, exchange and network. Therefore I think we need to take them even more seriously than the other exchanges / yield managers that are gaining traction out there (Rubicon, etc.).
context: Neal Mohan sizes up a small rival ad exchange after its product launch.

source.title: United States v. Google (ad tech), trial exhibit PTX0044, published by the Department of Justice

subject: Re: AdX TOS effectively prohibits publisher from using an adserver?
excerpt: This was a strategic decision. We allow redirection from 3rd party ad servers, but not from other exchanges or yield managers. Why? Because if we did then those systems would immediately have a super set of demand - anything the SSP had + all of AdX (including AdWords). No one would sign up for AdX directly.
context: A Google ad exchange product lead explains why AdX rules blocked rival exchanges from calling it.

source.title: United States v. Google (ad tech), trial exhibit PTX0128, published by the Department of Justice

His other feedback was that i) we should not pro-actively amend existing MADA's; adjusting language at renewal is fine, and ii) he'd like to soften the MADA to make it more gentle. We also discussed that the OEM search revenue share deals is a good place to re-insert this kind of language/commitment.
